questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
questions.context: When a country switches its organ-donation policy from "opt-in" (donation only if you actively register) to "opt-out" (donation unless you actively refuse), donation rates rise dramatically, often from under 15 percent of the population to over 90 percent, with no change whatsoever in the underlying willingness of citizens to donate. Almost no one, it turns out, revisits a pre-selected box once it has been ticked on their behalf. The default option is not a neutral starting point that people freely deviate from; for the overwhelming majority, the default simply becomes the decision, mistaken for effort not worth expending or, more quietly, for an implicit recommendation from whoever designed the form.

options.text: Why Some Countries Have More Willing Organ Donors Than Others
The Ethics of Mandatory Organ Donation Policy
How a Silent Default Option Can Determine a Nation's Choices
The History of Consent Law in Modern Medicine
Why Citizens Actively Resist Government-Designed Forms

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: A supermarket that stocks six varieties of jam sells more jam, in absolute terms, than one stocking twenty-four varieties, even though the larger display draws more browsers and more expressions of interest. Confronted with two dozen similar-looking jars, shoppers linger, compare, and — a disproportionate number of the time — walk away having bought nothing at all, apparently unable to justify any single choice when so many unexamined alternatives remain. Reduce the assortment to a manageable handful, and the same shoppers convert to buyers at several times the rate, seemingly relieved rather than deprived by the narrower set of options in front of them.

options.text: why supermarkets prefer selling jam over other condiments
how offering fewer options can paradoxically increase purchase rates
the manufacturing process behind different jam varieties
consumer preference for well-known jam brands over new ones
the history of supermarket shelf design

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: Bacteria exposed to a sublethal dose of an antibiotic do not merely fail to die; a small fraction, carrying a chance mutation that happens to confer resistance, survive and reproduce, passing that resistance to an entire subsequent generation within hours. Because bacterial generations are so short and their populations so large, a resistant strain can come to dominate a hospital ward's bacterial population within a single course of incompletely administered treatment. The evolutionary pressure is not created by antibiotics in general but specifically by their partial, inconsistent use — a course stopped early, a dose diluted, an environment where the drug is present just long enough to eliminate competitors without eliminating the resistant few.

options.text: the discovery of the first antibiotic compound
how incomplete or inconsistent antibiotic use accelerates the evolution of resistant bacteria
the total number of bacterial species found in hospitals
why hospitals should stop using antibiotics altogether
methods for diagnosing bacterial infections accurately

questions.text: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
questions.context: Ask someone to explain, in detail, how a zipper works, or how a toilet flushes, and confidence collapses almost immediately once the explanation must move past the first sentence. Most people rate their understanding of everyday mechanisms as fairly high until asked to actually produce the mechanism's inner workings step by step, at which point the gap between a fluent, gist-level familiarity and genuine causal understanding becomes impossible to ignore. Researchers call this the illusion of explanatory depth: a sense of comprehension borrowed, unknowingly, from having merely seen a thing function reliably many times, rather than from any grasp of why it functions at all.

options.text: People generally understand mechanical devices better than they think they do.
Familiarity with how something behaves is often mistaken for understanding why it behaves that way.
Toilets and zippers are the most commonly misunderstood mechanical devices.
Confidence in one's knowledge always increases after a detailed explanation is attempted.
Genuine causal understanding is impossible to acquire for most everyday mechanisms.

questions.text: How many of the statements below do NOT agree with the passage?
questions.context:
For years, I dreaded speaking in any meeting larger than three people, certain that a shaking voice would be noticed and judged the moment I opened my mouth. What finally helped wasn't a confidence trick or a breathing exercise, but a colleague's offhand comment that she found my "thoughtful pauses" reassuring, since they meant I was actually considering what to say rather than filling air. I had spent years treating my pauses as evidence of failure, when at least one listener had read the exact same behaviour as a sign of care. I still feel the same flutter of nerves before speaking today. What changed is that I no longer assume the flutter is visible, or that visibility would be catastrophic if it were.

Statements
(a) The writer overcame the nervousness itself before changing how she interpreted it.
(b) A colleague's comment revealed that a listener had interpreted the writer's pauses positively.
(c) The writer had previously assumed her pauses were read as a sign of weakness.
(d) The writer no longer experiences any nervousness before speaking.
(e) The writer changed her assumption about whether her nervousness was visible or catastrophic.
(f) The writer's change came primarily from a specific breathing technique.

questions.text: Which statement does NOT agree with the two explanations given in the passage?
questions.context: Several songbird species are accomplished vocal mimics, weaving the calls of other birds, and occasionally mechanical sounds, into their own songs. One explanation holds that mimicry functions primarily as a display of cognitive ability aimed at potential mates: a male capable of reproducing a large, varied repertoire of borrowed sounds demonstrates superior learning capacity and memory, traits a discerning female might reasonably value in a partner. A second, competing explanation proposes that mimicry instead serves a defensive function, deterring rival males from entering a territory by inflating, through vocal variety alone, the apparent number of different birds already present and defending it.

options.text: The first explanation treats mimicry as a signal of the male's cognitive and learning ability.
The first explanation suggests females may value the traits that mimicry demonstrates.
The second explanation proposes that mimicry deters rivals by suggesting a territory is more crowded than it is.
The second explanation agrees with the first that mimicry's primary function is attracting a mate.
Both explanations attempt to account for the same observed behaviour of vocal mimicry.

questions.text: Which of the following best explains the meaning of the underlined phrase "the curse of knowledge"?
questions.context: An experienced pianist asked to teach a rank beginner routinely underestimates how many steps the beginner will need, having long since forgotten what it felt like not to know which finger goes where. This is not arrogance; the expert genuinely cannot easily reconstruct their own earlier state of ignorance, a phenomenon researchers term _the curse of knowledge_. It afflicts textbook authors who omit steps obvious only to themselves, engineers who write instructions no novice could follow, and any expert, in any field, tasked with explaining their expertise to someone who does not yet share it.

options.text: a tendency for experts to deliberately withhold key information from beginners
a tendency for experts to overestimate how difficult a skill actually is
a difficulty experts have in imagining what it is like not to already know something
a curse specifically affecting musicians who teach children

questions.context: The division of labour, from which so many advantages are derived, does not originally proceed from any human wisdom which ① _prevents_ the general opulence to which it gives occasion. It is the necessary, though very slow and gradual, ② _consequence_ of a certain propensity in human nature: the propensity to truck, barter, and exchange one thing for another. Whether this propensity be one of those original principles in human nature which cannot be further accounted for, or whether it be the necessary ③ _consequence_ of reason and speech, is not our present business to inquire. It is common to all men, and to be found in no other race of animals. Two greyhounds, in running down the same hare, sometimes ④ _appear to cooperate_ as if by an agreement, but this is a common effect of a passion directed to the same object, not of a genuine contract between them. Nobody ever saw a dog make a ⑤ _fair and deliberate exchange_ of one bone for another with another dog.

questions.text: Which of the following questions CANNOT be answered from the passage?
questions.context: Elephants communicate over distances of several kilometres using infrasound, low-frequency rumbles pitched below the threshold of human hearing, which travel efficiently through both open air and the ground itself. A herd separated by dense vegetation or considerable distance can coordinate movement, warn of danger, or signal reproductive readiness entirely outside human perception, which is why observers for decades underestimated how socially connected apparently isolated elephant groups actually were. Researchers now use buried seismic sensors, originally designed to detect earthquakes, to pick up the ground-borne component of these calls and track herd movements no visible survey could reveal.

Subsequent research across other domains has found that the role of deliberate practice ⑤ _varies_ considerably, mattering enormously in some fields and comparatively little in others.

questions.context: Accident investigators increasingly describe major failures using the "Swiss cheese model": imagine several slices of cheese lined up in a row, each riddled with its own randomly placed holes, representing a different layer of safeguard — a warning system, a maintenance check, a trained operator, a backup mechanism. Any single slice, on its own, is full of gaps and would stop nothing. A catastrophic failure occurs only when ________. Add enough independent slices, each with holes in different places, and the odds of every hole aligning at once become vanishingly small, which is precisely why investigators searching for "the one cause" of a disaster so often come away disappointed, finding instead a chain of small, ordinary failures that happened to align.

the holes in several successive slices happen to align, allowing a clear path straight through

Interviewed afterward, many report having simply "known" the right action to take, with no memory of consciously comparing alternatives at all. Researchers studying this pattern have concluded that what looks like intuition is in fact (A) . Because the firefighter's brain has, across hundreds of prior fires, built a dense library of situation-action patterns, a new situation is instantly matched against that library, and the appropriate response surfaces without ever passing through deliberate, effortful comparison. A true novice, lacking that library entirely, cannot access this shortcut and so (B) , exactly the kind of explicit weighing the veteran appears to skip entirely.

questions.context: Decision researchers have long noted that people respond very differently to two descriptions of an identical outcome, depending only on whether that outcome is presented as a gain or as a loss. ( ① ) Told that a medical procedure has a "90 percent survival rate," patients and physicians alike judge it considerably more favourably than when told the mathematically identical procedure has a "10 percent mortality rate." ( ② ) The information conveyed is exactly the same; only the frame around it differs. ( ③ ) This asymmetry is not limited to medicine: identical policy outcomes are judged more harshly when described in terms of jobs lost than when described in terms of an equivalent number of jobs saved. ( ④ ) Marketers and policymakers alike have learned that the choice of frame, entirely apart from any change in substance, can shift public reaction substantially. ( ⑤ )

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate place for the given sentence: "Mere repeated exposure to a stimulus, entirely absent any reward or new information attached to it, is sufficient to increase how much a person likes it."
questions.context: In one classic study, participants were briefly shown a series of unfamiliar shapes and nonsense syllables, some repeated many times across the session and others shown only once. ( ① ) Afterward, asked simply to rate how much they liked each item, participants consistently rated the frequently repeated shapes and syllables more favourably than the ones seen only once. ( ② ) None of the participants could reliably report which items had actually been repeated, ruling out a simple memory-based explanation. ( ③ ) Researchers call this the mere-exposure effect, and it has since been documented across music, faces, and even the letters of one's own name, which people rate slightly more favourably than other letters of the alphabet. ( ④ ) Advertisers exploit this reliably, favouring sheer repetition of a brand name over persuasive argument in many campaigns. ( ⑤ )

questions.text: Arrange sentences ①–⑤ so that they fit the passage. Which sentence should come fourth?

Psychologists have proposed that the mind operates through two distinct modes of thought, often labeled simply System 1 and System 2.

① System 2, by contrast, is slow, deliberate, and effortful, engaged only when a problem resists the quick, automatic response System 1 supplies.

Offered a fifty-fifty gamble to either gain 100 dollars or lose 100 dollars, most people decline, even though the expected value of the gamble is exactly zero and a purely rational calculator of expected value should be indifferent to taking it. Losing 100 dollars, it turns out, registers as roughly twice as painful, psychologically, as gaining 100 dollars registers as pleasurable. Only when the potential gain is roughly double the potential loss does the average person become willing to accept the gamble, a ratio remarkably stable across countries, income levels, and the specific amounts involved, suggesting a deep asymmetry in how gains and losses are weighted rather than a simple failure of arithmetic.

In a staged emergency, a lone bystander who witnesses someone collapse almost always intervenes, calling for help or attempting aid within moments. Add several additional bystanders to the same staged scene, all of whom likewise merely observe rather than act, and the likelihood that any single person intervenes drops sharply, sometimes to a fraction of the lone-witness rate, even though the objective severity of the emergency has not changed at all.
